activities.caption: guess the magnitude — how empty is the atom?
activities.name: qftEmptyEst

config.prompt: An atom measures about 10⁻¹⁰ m across; its nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m. The nucleus is roughly how many times smaller than the atom?
config.why: 100,000 times smaller — yet it carries over 99.9% of the mass in 10⁻¹⁴ of the volume. Rutherford's alpha particles found it: as shocking as a 15-inch shell bouncing off tissue paper.
config.context: The electron weighs 1/1,836 of a proton — the nucleus holds essentially all the mass.

activities.anchor: atoms are mostly empty space, so matter is mostly nothing
activities.caption: true or false — what the 'empty' space actually is
activities.name: qftEmptyJudge

statements.s: Atoms are mostly emptiness, so matter is mostly nothing.
statements.why: The space is filled with the electron's wavefunction and the electromagnetic field it sustains — matter is mostly field.

statements.s: Your hand stops at a table partly because electrons in skin and surface cannot occupy the same quantum states.
statements.why: Pauli exclusion — and the fields repel before nuclei ever touch.

statements.s: This 'filled emptiness' is exactly what resists compression.
statements.why: Which is why solids push back: the fields are what you have been touching all along.

statements.s: All electrons are identical because they happen to be manufactured identically.
statements.why: They are the same field, plucked twice — literal sameness of the underlying field.

activities.caption: file each emission under its fundamental force
activities.name: qftEmissionSort

config.prompt: Three emissions, three forces — file each fact:

items.label: a helium nucleus — 2 protons, 2 neutrons — the strong force losing a fragment
stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air
an electron from the nucleus — the weak force converting a neutron
Pauli predicted its ghostly partner, the neutrino, in 1930
a high-energy photon, no mass — the first QFT fact in the syllabus

config.why: The sorting is a map of three fundamental forces — and gamma rays being photons means light is quantised, proven in the syllabus itself.

activities.anchor: the syllabus's encounter with genuine quantum randomness
activities.caption: place the marker at the sample's age in half-lives
activities.name: qftC14Place

config.prompt: Carbon-14 (half-life 5,730 years) dates organic remains. A sample retains 25% of the atmospheric proportion — place the marker at its age in half-lives:
config.why: Half remains after one half-life, a quarter after two — ≈ 11,460 years; 12.5% gives ≈ 17,190. λ ≈ 1.21 × 10⁻⁴ per year, so a single atom has about a one-in-8,000 chance of decaying in any given year.

activities.anchor: half-life means the substance is safe after two
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's waste-handling note
activities.name: qftWasteSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's waste-handling note is wrong — click it:
lines: After one half-life, half the original activity remains; after two, a quarter.
A quarter is not zero — 'ten half-lives' (about 1/1,000 left) is the usual waste-handling benchmark for long-lived isotopes.
After two half-lives the danger has dropped 75%, so the material is now safe.
Exponential decay means 'smaller, fast at first, then slower forever' — never a clean endpoint.
Some isotopes need centuries of handling before they are genuinely negligible.
config.correction: A quarter of the activity remains — 'safe after two half-lives' is exactly wrong, and the reverse panic is equally wrong: exponential decay never offers a clean endpoint.
config.why: Smaller, fast at first, then slower forever — the ensemble law is perfect while each individual decay stays quantum-random.

activities.caption: pair each detector with its trade-off
activities.name: qftDetectorMatch

config.prompt: How the invisible becomes a number — pair each detector with its trade:

pairs.right: an avalanche counted pulse by pulse — energy-blind but dead-reliable
flashes when struck; the flash's brightness carries the energy — sensitivity traded for spectroscopy
condensation or boiling along the ionisation trail — how the particle zoo was charted
tracking chambers in a magnetic field give momentum; calorimeters take total energy; muon detectors catch the only particles that get that far

config.why: The principle every layer shares: radiation is detected by the charge it knocks loose — measurement is avalanche plus statistics.

activities.anchor: where emission physics meets human biology
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the three dose units
activities.name: qftDoseCloze

config.text: Activity (in %%0%%) counts decays per second; absorbed dose (in %%1%%) counts energy deposited per kilogram; effective dose (in %%2%%) weights by biological damage — a gray of alpha inside the body is roughly twenty times more damaging than a gray of gamma.
config.hint: One unit per question: how many events, how much energy, how much harm.

activities.anchor: all radiation is equally dangerous, so a granite worktop is a Chernobyl
activities.caption: drag the divider — two doses, two universes of harm
activities.name: qftDoseCompare

config.prompt: Danger scales with activity, energy, emission type and location — drag to compare the extremes:

before.label: a banana (potassium-40)
before.text: About 0.1 μSv — natural background itself runs 2–3 millisieverts per year worldwide, roughly half of it radon gas.

after.label: a milligray of internal alpha
after.text: Alpha's dense ionisation track does concentrated local harm — roughly twenty times more damaging per gray than gamma inside the body. Radon in poorly ventilated homes is the leading cause of lung cancer among non-smokers.

config.why: The physics doesn't do adjectives; it does numbers, and the numbers are measured per case.
